Zudilin's Forms at Rational Bases: Proofs and Research Record

Erdős #1049

Native MathML copy. For the TeX-rendered copy with linked references, read the exact-TeX version.

Introduction

Let t>1t>1 be a rational number and let τ(n)\tau(n) count the divisors of nn. Erdős Problem #1049 asks whether F(t)=∑n≥11tn−1=∑n≥1τ(n)tnF(t)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{t^{n}-1}=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\tau(n)}{t^{n}} is irrational [2].

The two series agree by expanding (tn−1)−1=∑k≥1t−nk(t^{n}-1)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge1}t^{-nk} and collecting equal exponents. Nonnegativity justifies the rearrangement, while τ(m)≤m\tau(m)\le m proves absolute convergence for every real t>1t>1. With q=1/tq=1/t, the same function is the qq-harmonic series ∑n≥1qn/(1−qn)\sum_{n\ge1}q^n/(1-q^n). Chowla conjectured that the answer is yes for every rational t>1t>1. Erdős proved the integer case t≥2t\ge2 in 1948 [1]; the rational-base question is recorded in the catalogue . The full conjecture remains open.

We specialise Zudilin’s 2004 construction [8] to prove irrationality whenever a>b≥1a>b\ge1 are coprime and log⁡b/log⁡a<θ*=0.40568302138406054…\log b/\log a<\theta^{*}=0.40568302138406054\ldots. This includes 31/431/4 and every positive integral power of 31/431/4. Earlier results already treat noninteger rational bases, including 7/27/2; the point here is the explicit condition obtained from these particular forms, not a first noninteger example.

For a reduced positive fraction r/sr/s with r>s≥1r>s\ge1, its height is max⁡(r,s)=r\max(r,s)=r. Among noninteger rational numbers greater than one, 3/23/2 has the smallest height. It is also outside both the region proved here and the region of Bundschuh and Väänänen [6], which contains 7/27/2. We use 3/23/2 to examine why clearing denominators can destroy an otherwise small approximation error.

The denominator cost can be read from the degrees. If U,V∈ℤ[X]U,V\in\mathbb{Z}[X] have degree at most WW, then bWU(a/b)b^WU(a/b) and bWV(a/b)b^WV(a/b) are integers. For this clearing argument, a small remainder U(a/b)F(a/b)−V(a/b)U(a/b)F(a/b)-V(a/b) must remain small after multiplication by bWb^W. Cancelling a common polynomial factor first can reduce this cost. For example, the pair (X+1)(X+2),(X+1)(X+3)(X+1)(X+2),(X+1)(X+3) gives the cleared pair (35,45)(35,45) at 3/23/2 with degree bound 22; after cancelling X+1X+1, degree bound 11 gives (7,9)(7,9). These illustrative polynomials are not approximants to FF.

For the actual polynomials, Section 2 proves log⁡(bWn(Un(a/b)F(a/b)−Vn(a/b)))=(C1log⁡b−C0log⁡a)n2+o(n2),\log\!\left(b^{W_n}\bigl(U_n(a/b)F(a/b)-V_n(a/b)\bigr)\right) =\bigl(C_1\log b-C_0\log a\bigr)n^2+o(n^2), with a positive expression inside the logarithm. Here Wn=deg⁡UnW_n=\deg U_n and deg⁡Vn=Wn−1\deg V_n=W_n-1; the constants are defined in that section. A negative coefficient of n2n^2 makes the positive values of these integer-coefficient forms tend to zero. If F(a/b)F(a/b) were rational, multiplication by its fixed denominator would give positive integers tending to zero, a contradiction.

The Hankel determinant uses a different remainder sequence, from Zudilin’s 2016 construction. Its proof begins in Section 3.1. We first compute its least nonzero power of qq by row operations, then prove a separate estimate at fixed real qq. Neither argument transfers the cyclotomic factors of the 2004 polynomials to this determinant.

The shorter companion, Zudilin’s Forms at Rational Bases and the Exact Normalised Hankel Order, gives the principal proofs in Sections 2 and 3; neither uses its supplementary Section 4. Here Section 3.3 contains separate coefficient-moment and spectral calculations, not inputs to the order formula. Sections 4–5 compare rescaling integer rows with imposing congruences by addition; Sections 6–7 examine partial sums. Sections 8–9 treat 7/27/2 and a specified denominator-exponent model. Section 10 distinguishes a reformulation of irrationality from questions about specified families, with an example of a nonzero remainder that does not decay after division. Literature comparisons follow, and Appendix A separates formal proofs from finite computations.

Links in the running text go to Lean proofs of single steps, such as a finite inequality; such a link does not cover the surrounding argument.

All logarithms are natural. Empty products and determinants equal 11. A subscripted constant in Ox(⋅)O_x(\cdot) may depend on the fixed base xx. We introduce the notation for each construction locally.

Keywords. irrationality; Lambert series; rational base; Padé approximation; Lean 4. MSC 2020. 11J72 (primary); 11J82, 68V20 (secondary).

The proof below needs JJ in its combinatorial form as well. Put ω(ξ)=max⁡{0,⌊14ξ⌋+⌊13ξ⌋−⌊12ξ⌋−⌊15ξ⌋,2⌊14ξ⌋−⌊13ξ⌋−⌊15ξ⌋},\omega(\xi)=\max\bigl\{0,\; \lfloor14\xi\rfloor+\lfloor13\xi\rfloor-\lfloor12\xi\rfloor-\lfloor15\xi\rfloor,\; 2\lfloor14\xi\rfloor-\lfloor13\xi\rfloor-\lfloor15\xi\rfloor\bigr\}, the weight that [8] attaches to the six-tuple c=(13,14,12,14,15,13)c=(13,14,12,14,15,13) for the chosen parameter ratios; it gives the exponents νl=ω(n/l)\nu_l=\omega(n/l) of the source’s (22) and enters its limit (26). Lemma 2.1 (the weight is an indicator). On [0,1)[0,1) the function ω\omega takes only the values 00 and 11, and ω=1\omega=1 exactly on the union of the thirteen half-open intervals listed above.

Proof. Each of the three expressions inside the maximum is constant on every interval between consecutive elements of {k/c:c∈{12,13,14,15},0≤k≤c}\{k/c: c\in\{12,13,14,15\},\ 0\le k\le c\}, since those are the only points at which one of the four floor functions changes. There are 4848 such intervals in [0,1)[0,1); evaluating ω\omega at the midpoint of each gives the value 11 on the thirteen listed half-open intervals and 00 elsewhere, and the thirteen listed intervals are unions of consecutive cells. Each floor function is right-continuous, so a cell has the same value at its left endpoint as at its midpoint. This also verifies the half-open endpoint convention. All evaluations use exact rational arithmetic. ◻

Lemma 2.1 and termwise integration of the positive series −ψ1′(ξ)=∑k≥02(k+ξ)−3-\psi_1'(\xi)=\sum_{k\ge0}2(k+\xi)^{-3} give the two forms of JJ used below, J=∫01ω(ξ)∑k≥02(k+ξ)3dξ=∑i=113(ψ1(ui)−ψ1(vi)),J=\int_0^1\omega(\xi)\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{2}{(k+\xi)^{3}}\,d\xi =\sum_{i=1}^{13}\bigl(\psi_1(u_i)-\psi_1(v_i)\bigr), the first being the integral ∫01ωd(−ψ1)\int_0^1\omega\,d(-\psi_1) of [8]. Since ω\omega vanishes near 00, both are finite.

For b=1b=1 the logarithmic ratio is zero, so the condition includes every integer base. For b>1b>1 it requires a>b2.46497868…a>b^{2.46497868\ldots}, substantially more than a>ba>b. There are still infinitely many admissible coprime numerators for each fixed denominator. The base 31/431/4 is included, whereas 3/23/2 is excluded. Taking positive integral powers does not change the ratio. At equality with the cutoff, the estimates give no conclusion.

Theorem 2.2 (rational-base region). Let a>b≥1a>b\ge1 be coprime integers with bμ<a,equivalentlylog⁡blog⁡a<θ*=0.40568302138406054…b^{\mu}<a, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \frac{\log b}{\log a}<\theta^{*}=0.40568302138406054\ldots Then F(a/b)=∑m≥1((a/b)m−1)−1F(a/b)=\sum_{m\ge1}(( a/b)^{m}-1)^{-1} is irrational.

The proof has three steps. We cancel the common polynomial factors using Zudilin’s integrality argument [8]. We then compute the degree of the remaining polynomials, using his cyclotomic limits and the reciprocal-interval method of [7]. Finally, we evaluate at a/ba/b and show that the positive remainder still decays after multiplication by the required power of bb. These steps occupy Sections 2.1–2.4. The construction, direction and constants are Zudilin’s; the rational specialisation and its degree and remainder estimates are proved below.

The source’s proof supplies the polynomial form. Its Lemma 4 (pp. 157–159) clears the two rational coefficients separately by Gaussian-binomial identities in ℤ[X]\mathbb{Z}[X]. Second, the module inclusion gives a polynomial coefficient pair, and uniqueness identifies it with the displayed cancelled source pair. For a reduced fraction a/ba/b, the unit leading coefficient also gives the exact denominator of Un(a/b)U_n(a/b), not just an upper bound. Applying the same prime-by-prime reduction at its own degree shows that Vn(a/b)V_n(a/b) has reduced denominator exactly bWn−1b^{W_n-1}. Thus bWnb^{W_n} is the least common clearing denominator, although the second coordinate alone needs one fewer power of bb. In the common normalisation, gcd⁡(bWnVn(a/b),bWn)=b.\gcd\!\bigl(b^{W_n}V_n(a/b),b^{W_n}\bigr)=b. Indeed bWnVn(a/b)b^{W_n}V_n(a/b) is bb times an integer coprime to bb. These facts concern the fixed source pair, not all approximants. The degree calculation fixes nn and varies xx; the decay calculation fixes xx and varies nn.

The cyclotomic limit

The limits proved in this subsection are those of . The proof splits the condition {n/l}∈[u,v)\{n/l\}\in[u,v) into reciprocal blocks and applies the summatory totient estimate on each, as in the proof of [7], and adds an explicit truncation estimate.

Write Σn=∑2≤l≤Nνn,lφ(l)\Sigma_n=\sum_{2\le l\le N}\nu_{n,l}\varphi(l). The elementary summatory estimate is ∑l≤yφ(l)=3π−2y2+O(ylog⁡(2y))\sum_{l\le y}\varphi(l)=3\pi^{-2}y^{2}+O(y\log(2y)). The condition {n/l}∈[u,v)\{n/l\}\in[u,v) holds exactly on the blocks nk+v<l≤nk+u,k=0,1,2,…,\frac{n}{k+v}<l\le\frac{n}{k+u},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots, so the summatory estimate gives, for each fixed kk, n−2∑l in block kφ(l)→3π−2((k+u)−2−(k+v)−2)n^{-2}\sum_{l\text{ in block }k}\varphi(l)\to3\pi^{-2}\bigl((k+u)^{-2}-(k+v)^{-2}\bigr). For L≥1L\ge1, all blocks with k≥Lk\ge L lie below n/(L+u)n/(L+u). For every y≥0y\ge0, ∑l≤yφ(l)≤y2.\sum_{l\le y}\varphi(l)\le y^2. For y<1y<1 the sum is empty; otherwise it is at most ⌊y⌋(⌊y⌋+1)/2≤y2\lfloor y\rfloor(\lfloor y\rfloor+1)/2\le y^2. Taking n→∞n\to\infty first and then L→∞L\to\infty justifies the infinite block sum, and summing the thirteen half-open intervals gives n−2Σn→3J/π2n^{-2}\Sigma_n\to3J/\pi^{2}. Proofs, earlier work and limitations

Formal verification and computations.

The printed proofs of Theorems 2.2 and 2.3 use Zudilin’s construction: his Lemma 7 in its polynomial reading, together with the inputs of that lemma’s own proof, namely his Lemma 3, the exponent M(a;b)M(a;b) of (16) proved by his Lemma 4, the group stability of his Lemma 5, and the identity (9)–(11), all in [8], and his direction and constants . Proved here are the nonrationality of FF as a function, the identification of the polynomial coefficients in Lemma 7, the exact degrees of UnU_n and VnV_n, positivity, the Archimedean size estimate, and the limit (Kn−Wn)/n2→C0(K_n-W_n)/n^{2}\to C_0. That last limit rests on Zudilin’s Lemmas 1 and 2 [8], whose method goes back to ; Section 2.3 proves them by that method with an explicit truncation estimate. Lean proves both theorems and the measure bound of Corollary 2.4; it constructs the polynomials and proves their remainder estimates. The Lean sources also contain the finite comparisons, the rational bracket in Section 2.5 and the degree identities in Section 2.2. Appendix A distinguishes these proofs from computer algebra.

Exact computations outside Lean certify the rational interval bounds, Un,VnU_n,V_n for 1≤n≤41\le n\le4, the sixteen coefficient-positivity tests through rank eight, and the finite parameter search. The five complete polynomial contents and seventy-six residue certificates are described in Section 3.3. The historical high-precision real remainder evaluations are separate numerical reports, not reproduced by these exact computations. None of these finite computations is needed for the proof of Theorem 2.2.

Attribution.

Bundschuh and Väänänen proved the irrationality of F(a/b)F(a/b) on the region log⁡b/log⁡a<1/2−1/π2=0.3986788163576622…\log b/\log a<1/2-1/\pi^{2}=0.3986788163576622\ldots [6], and every base of Theorem 2.2 with b≤3b\le3 is already theirs. Their printed hypothesis for α=−1\alpha=-1 is λ<(1/2+1/π2)−1\lambda<(1/2+1/\pi^{2})^{-1} with λ=log⁡h(q)/log⁡|q|\lambda=\log h(q)/\log|q|. Here the source uses qq for the base, not its reciprocal, and Eq(z)=∏j≥1(1+zq−j),Lq(z)=Eq′(z)Eq(z)=∑j≥11qj+z.E_q(z)=\prod_{j\ge1}(1+zq^{-j}),\qquad L_q(z)=\frac{E_q'(z)}{E_q(z)}=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac1{q^j+z}. For q=a/b>1q=a/b>1, Eq(−1)>0E_q(-1)>0 and Lq(−1)=F(a/b)L_q(-1)=F(a/b); in particular α=−1\alpha=-1 is not one of the excluded zeros −qj-q^j. Since a,ba,b are coprime and a>b>0a>b>0, the rational height is h(q)=ah(q)=a. Thus λ=log⁡a/log⁡(a/b)=1/(1−log⁡b/log⁡a)\lambda=\log a/\log(a/b)=1/(1-\log b/\log a), and the printed hypothesis is equivalent to the displayed inequality. Duverney proved another, strictly smaller, region for the same series [13]. Zudilin remarked that his generalized qq-logarithm results can be given at non-integer rational bases under an assumption log⁡|r|>clog⁡|s|\log|r|>c\log|s| for a computable c>0c>0, without computing a value [9]. Zudilin’s 2004 paper supplies the forms and the exponent μ\mu under the standing hypothesis p=1/q∈ℤ∖{0,±1}p=1/q\in\mathbb{Z}\mathbin{\backslash}\{0,\pm1\}, and it states no rational-base result [8]. The contribution here is the rational specialisation of the 2004 forms, with the denominator accounting and the limit passage carried out in full, which identifies the printed μ\mu as an admissible cc for FF itself, together with the region that constant defines and its application to 31/431/4.

Where the earlier criterion stops.

Both regions are cut out by the same quantity. The published cutoff 1/2−1/π21/2-1/\pi^{2} of [6] is the reciprocal of μBV=2π2/(π2−2)\mu_{\mathrm{BV}}=2\pi^{2}/(\pi^{2}-2), the constant Van Assche later recovered as an integer-base irrationality-exponent bound for F(p)F(p) [17], and the cutoff θ*\theta^{*} of Theorem 2.2 is the reciprocal of the smaller integer-base bound μ=C1/C0\mu=C_1/C_0 printed at [8]. For Zudilin’s family this reciprocal relation uses both the exact degree limit d=C1−C0d=C_1-C_0 and the stronger evaluation bound |Un(p)|≤pWnexp⁡(Op(n))|U_n(p)|\le p^{W_n}\exp(O_p(n)) proved in Corollary 2.4, together with decay exponent σ=C0\sigma=C_0. A general exponential coefficient-height bound would contribute an additional term to the integer-base exponent estimate; it cannot simply be discarded. The discussion following Theorem 2.5 makes that distinction explicit. The rational-base proof clears the denominators of the already cancelled polynomials. It does not infer value irrationality merely by taking the reciprocal of a published exponent bound. The bases gained are exactly the strip sμ<r≤sμBVs^{\mu}<r\le s^{\mu_{\mathrm{BV}}}, which is empty for s=2s=2 and s=3s=3 and is first occupied at s=4s=4 by the single coprime numerator 3131. The integer comparisons and rational bracket in Section 2.5 establish membership in the region. The irrationality conclusion in Theorem 2.3 also uses the constructed forms and their proved analytic estimates. This application does not improve either inherited integer-base exponent bound.

What a larger region would require.

At 3/23/2 the logarithmic parameter is log⁡2log⁡3=0.6309297535714574…,\frac{\log2}{\log3}=0.6309297535714574\ldots, which exceeds θ*\theta^* by 0.2252467…0.2252467\ldots. Theorem 2.2 gives no conclusion when log⁡b/log⁡a≥θ*\log b/\log a\ge\theta^*. The same argument can apply to another family once its polynomial integrality, degrees and fixed-base remainder estimates are proved. A smaller ratio of the resulting constants C1/C0C_1/C_0 would enlarge the reciprocal-cutoff region. For example, C1/C0≤2.4234C_1/C_0\le2.4234 would give a cutoff greater than 0.41260.4126 and admit 29/429/4. An integer-base irrationality-exponent bound alone does not supply the polynomial data needed for this specialisation. The existing formal proofs establish irrationality and measure bounds for the constructed forms; they do not supply a different family whose divided remainder is small and nonzero at 3/23/2.

The following condition is stronger than having estimates at 3/23/2: one polynomial family must work at every fixed x>1x>1 with the same leading constants. The error terms may depend on xx. The 2004 family above satisfies these hypotheses. Estimates for that family at only one base, or for a different family at each base, do not verify them. The conclusion concerns these two-coordinate linear forms, not simultaneous forms in several independent target values. Here height means the largest absolute coefficient. The short paper uses the sum of the absolute coefficients; for a polynomial of degree at most dd, maxj|pj|≤∑j|pj|≤(d+1)maxj|pj|.\max_j|p_j|\le\sum_j|p_j|\le(d+1)\max_j|p_j|. For a nonzero polynomial of degree d=O(n2)d=O(n^2), the logarithms of these norms differ by O(log⁡n)O(\log n). They have the same leading quadratic growth rate, but the literal zero-height conditions are not identical: 1+X1+X has maximum coefficient 11 and coefficient sum 22. In particular, when h=0h=0, the displayed bound hn2(1+o(1))hn^2(1+o(1)) is zero, not an arbitrary o(n2)o(n^2) term. The proof below also works with the additive bound hn2+o(n2)hn^2+o(n^2); its evaluation estimate absorbs the O(log⁡n)O(\log n) difference. Alternatively, either norm convention satisfies the other paper’s hypothesis after replacing hh by any larger positive constant. The degree conclusion is independent of that replacement. In the rational-base conclusions, write a/ba/b with integers a>b≥1a>b\ge1. The estimates hold without coprimality; a reduced representation gives the smaller denominator-clearing factor.

Theorem 2.5 (a degree restriction for estimates valid at every base). Let (Un,Vn)∈ℤ[x]2(U_n,V_n)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]^{2} be a sequence such that, for constants σ,δ>0\sigma,\delta>0 and h≥0h\ge0 independent of nn and of the base,

  1. Λn(x):=Un(x)F(x)−Vn(x)≠0\Lambda_n(x):=U_n(x)F(x)-V_n(x)\ne0 for every real x>1x>1;

  2. deg⁡Un,deg⁡Vn≤δn2(1+o(1))\deg U_n,\deg V_n\le\delta n^{2}(1+o(1));

  3. the coefficient heights satisfy log⁡max⁡(H(Un),H(Vn))≤hn2(1+o(1)),\log\max\bigl(H(U_n),H(V_n)\bigr)\le hn^{2}(1+o(1)), where H(P)H(P) is the largest absolute value of a coefficient of PP;

  4. the remainders satisfy log⁡|Λn(x)|=−σn2log⁡x(1+o(1))\log|\Lambda_n(x)|=-\sigma n^{2}\log x\,(1+o(1)) for every real x>1x>1.

Put dn:=max⁡(deg⁡Un,deg⁡Vn)d_n:=\max(\deg U_n,\deg V_n). Then σ≤δ\sigma\le\delta, and for every fixed rational base a/b>1a/b>1, limsupn→∞n−2log⁡|bdnΛn(a/b)|≤δlog⁡b−σlog⁡(a/b).\limsup_{n\to\infty}n^{-2}\log\bigl|b^{d_n}\Lambda_n(a/b)\bigr| \le\delta\log b-\sigma\log(a/b). Consequently the homogenised forms tend to zero whenever log⁡b/log⁡a<σ/(σ+δ)\log b/\log a<\sigma/(\sigma+\delta), a sufficient region whose cutoff is at most 1/21/2. If the actual degrees satisfy dn/n2→dd_n/n^{2}\to d, then d≥σd\ge\sigma and the limit exists and equals dlog⁡b−σlog⁡(a/b)d\log b-\sigma\log(a/b); in that case the forms tend to zero below log⁡b/log⁡a=σ/(σ+d)\log b/\log a=\sigma/(\sigma+d) and their absolute values tend to infinity above it, so the exact-degree case has no decaying homogenised forms at 3/23/2.

Proof. The coefficient-height bound controls evaluation at an integer base. For every fixed p>1p>1, |Un(p)|,|Vn(p)|≤(dn+1)max⁡(H(Un),H(Vn))pdn≤exp⁡((h+δlog⁡p)n2+o(n2)).|U_n(p)|,|V_n(p)| \le (d_n+1)\max(H(U_n),H(V_n))p^{d_n} \le \exp\bigl((h+\delta\log p)n^2+o(n^2)\bigr). Here log⁡(dn+1)=o(n2)\log(d_n+1)=o(n^2) by the degree bound. This is where the coefficient-height hypothesis is needed.

Suppose σ>δ\sigma>\delta and choose an integer p≥2p\ge2 such that (σ−δ)log⁡p>h(\sigma-\delta)\log p>h. Put un=Un(p)u_n=U_n(p), vn=Vn(p)v_n=V_n(p) and ℓn=unF(p)−vn\ell_n=u_nF(p)-v_n. The evaluation bound and hypothesis (4) give unvn+1−un+1vn=un+1ℓn−unℓn+1=o(1).u_nv_{n+1}-u_{n+1}v_n=u_{n+1}\ell_n-u_n\ell_{n+1}=o(1). Indeed, each product on the right has absolute value at most exp⁡((h+(δ−σ)log⁡p)n2+o(n2))\exp((h+(\delta-\sigma)\log p)n^2+o(n^2)). The expression on the left is an integer, so it is eventually zero. Also un≠0u_n\ne0 eventually, since un=0u_n=0 would make ℓn=−vn\ell_n=-v_n a nonzero integer of absolute value less than 11. Thus vn/unv_n/u_n is eventually a fixed rational number rr. If F(p)=rF(p)=r, then ℓn=0\ell_n=0; otherwise |ℓn|=|un||F(p)−r|≥|F(p)−r||\ell_n|=|u_n|\,|F(p)-r|\ge|F(p)-r|. Both contradict the nonzero remainders tending to zero. Hence σ≤δ\sigma\le\delta.

For a fixed rational base a/b>1a/b>1, taking logarithms gives n−2log⁡|bdnΛn(a/b)|=dnn2log⁡b−σlog⁡(a/b)+o(1).n^{-2}\log|b^{d_n}\Lambda_n(a/b)| =\frac{d_n}{n^2}\log b-\sigma\log(a/b)+o(1). Hypothesis (2) yields the stated upper limit and sufficient region. Since σ≤δ\sigma\le\delta, its cutoff is at most 1/21/2. If dn/n2→dd_n/n^2\to d, apply the preceding integer-base argument with d+εd+\varepsilon in place of δ\delta for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 to obtain d≥σd\ge\sigma. The displayed identity then gives the exact limit. Its sign is that of (σ+d)log⁡b−σlog⁡a(\sigma+d)\log b-\sigma\log a, which proves both assertions away from equality. At 3/23/2 this sign is positive because log⁡2/log⁡3>1/2≥σ/(σ+d)\log2/\log3>1/2\ge\sigma/(\sigma+d). ◻

Corollary 2.6 (nondecay when b<a<b2b<a<b^2). Under the hypotheses of Theorem 2.5, for positive integers a,ba,b with b<a<b2b<a<b^2, the undivided forms bdnΛn(a/b)b^{d_n}\Lambda_n(a/b) do not tend to zero. No limit of dn/n2d_n/n^2 is assumed.

Proof. Write x=a/bx=a/b and suppose Cn=bdnΛn(x)→0C_n=b^{d_n}\Lambda_n(x)\to0. Eventual nonvanishing gives log⁡|Cn|=dnlog⁡b+log⁡|Λn(x)|\log|C_n|=d_n\log b+\log|\Lambda_n(x)| for all sufficiently large nn. Also |Cn|≤1|C_n|\le1 eventually. The lower side of the remainder asymptotic therefore implies dnlog⁡b≤−log⁡|Λn(x)|=σlog⁡xn2+o(n2).d_n\log b\le-\log|\Lambda_n(x)| =\sigma\log x\,n^2+o(n^2). Set c=σlog⁡x/log⁡bc=\sigma\log x/\log b. Since 1<x<b1<x<b, we have 0<c<σ0<c<\sigma, and the displayed inequality gives dn≤(c+ε)n2d_n\le(c+\varepsilon)n^2 eventually for each ε>0\varepsilon>0. Apply Theorem 2.5 to the same family with degree upper rate cc. Its height bound, nonvanishing and remainder asymptotics at every real base greater than one are unchanged. The theorem gives σ≤c\sigma\le c, a contradiction. ◻

This strengthens the failure of a sufficient-cutoff test to an exclusion of decay under the stated all-base hypotheses. It does not supply an actual-degree limit or assert divergence. If dn/n2→dd_n/n^2\to d, the separate exact-degree result gives the stronger conclusion |bdnΛn(a/b)|→∞|b^{d_n}\Lambda_n(a/b)|\to\infty in the same strict region. Equality a=b2a=b^2 remains unclassified. The corollary concerns the undivided forms; it does not exclude base-dependent content division or other irrationality methods outside its hypotheses.

The coefficient-height hypothesis (3) supplies the evaluation bound used in this proof. A degree bound alone gives no such estimate: polynomials of degree zero can have arbitrarily large integer coefficients. The constant hh is independent of the base, which lets us choose one large integer pp with (σ−δ)log⁡p>h(\sigma-\delta)\log p>h under the contradiction hypothesis σ>δ\sigma>\delta. This explains the use of (3); it does not prove that the hypothesis cannot be weakened or omitted from the theorem. At the boundary log⁡b/log⁡a=σ/(σ+d)\log b/\log a=\sigma/(\sigma+d) the normalised logarithm is zero and these hypotheses decide neither behaviour. Theorem 2.5 constrains families satisfying its hypotheses and does not exclude every possible Padé construction.

There is also a distinction between the degree cutoff and an irrationality-exponent estimate at a fixed integer base p≥2p\ge2. The hypotheses above give |Un(p)|≤exp⁡((h+δlog⁡p)n2+o(n2)),|Λn(p)|=exp⁡(−σlog⁡pn2+o(n2)).|U_n(p)|\le\exp((h+\delta\log p)n^2+o(n^2)),\qquad |\Lambda_n(p)|=\exp(-\sigma\log p\,n^2+o(n^2)). Apply the integer-form argument in the proof of Corollary 2.4, with coefficient growth rate h+δlog⁡ph+\delta\log p and remainder decay rate σlog⁡p\sigma\log p. It gives μirr(F(p))≤1+δσ+hσlog⁡p.\mu_\mathrm{irr}(F(p))\le 1+\frac{\delta}{\sigma}+\frac{h}{\sigma\log p}. Thus the reciprocal σ/(σ+δ)\sigma/(\sigma+\delta) of the degree expression 1+δ/σ1+\delta/\sigma is not, under these hypotheses alone, the reciprocal of the exponent bound furnished by that argument. To obtain the latter identification it suffices to prove the stronger evaluated estimate |Un(p)|≤exp⁡(δlog⁡pn2+o(n2))|U_n(p)|\le\exp(\delta\log p\,n^2+o(n^2)). This is separate from bounding the polynomial’s coefficients by exp⁡(O(n2))\exp(O(n^2)).

For the family of Section 2.1 the fourth hypothesis is the size estimate proved there and the second is [long1049:eq:exact-degree]. The third is proved next, so Theorem 2.5 applies to that family.

Lemma 2.7 (coefficient heights of the constructed polynomials). There is a constant hh with log⁡max⁡(H(Un),H(Vn))≤hn2\log\max\bigl(H(U_n),H(V_n)\bigr)\le hn^{2} for every n≥1n\ge1, where UnU_n and VnV_n are the polynomials of [long1049:eq:integer-polynomial-pair].

With Lemma 2.7, Zudilin’s family satisfies all four hypotheses of Theorem 2.5, with exact degree limit d=C1−C0d=C_1-C_0 by [long1049:eq:degree-limits], and decay exponent σ=C0\sigma=C_0 because log⁡Λn(x)=−(Kn−Wn)log⁡x+o(n2)\log\Lambda_n(x)=-(K_n-W_n)\log x+o(n^{2}) for each fixed real x>1x>1 by the size estimate of Section 2.4. Examples of rational bases.

Among reduced a/ba/b with 1≤b<a≤601\le b<a\le60, the region of Theorem 2.2 has 137137 members, of which 7878 are non-integral. The two largest admitted logarithmic ratios belong to 53/553/5 and 31/431/4, respectively 0.0003130.000313 and 0.0019850.001985 below θ*\theta^*; the smallest excluded ratio is that of 52/552/5, namely 0.4073243836…0.4073243836\ldots, which exceeds the cutoff by 0.0016410.001641. A calculation with rational bounds for logarithms and for the cutoff checks all 11011101 reduced fractions in the stated range, these rounded margins and the four fixed-denominator comparisons below (program, result). The bases in this region and outside the region of are those in the strip sμ<r≤sμBVs^{\mu}<r\le s^{\mu_{\mathrm{BV}}}, which is empty for s=2s=2 and s=3s=3, is {31}\{31\} for s=4s=4, and is {53,54,56}\{53,54,56\} for s=5s=5. The strip is infinite: its width sμBV−sμs^{\mu_{\mathrm{BV}}}-s^{\mu} eventually exceeds ss, so for every large enough denominator it contains an integer congruent to 11 modulo ss. Hence 31/431/4 is the member of the strip with least denominator and least numerator.

A certified finite parameter search.

The parameter ratios (14,12,14;27)(14,12,14;27) are Zudilin’s [8]. They maximise C0/C1C_0/C_1 in the following finite box: positive integer parameters (α0,α1,α2;β)(\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\alpha_2;\beta) with every entry at most 3030, greatest common divisor 11, and α1≤α2,α1+α2<β≤α0+α2.\alpha_1\le\alpha_2,\qquad \alpha_1+\alpha_2<\beta\le\alpha_0+\alpha_2. These are the source’s parameter inequalities [8], with a bound imposed for enumeration. The definitions of C0,C1C_0,C_1 and their floor function are reproduced in Section 10. There are exactly 37,53337{,}533 tuples. Exactly two attain the maximum: (14,12,14;27)(14,12,14;27) and (15,12,13;26)(15,12,13;26). Both give θ*\theta^*, although they are distinct primitive directions.

The enumeration and comparisons are certified by rational intervals. The fractions j/cj/c with 1≤c≤301\le c\le30 partition [0,1)[0,1) into 278278 half-open intervals. Every floor function occurring in the search is constant on each interval, and the first interval contributes zero. On each remaining interval [u,v)[u,v), the integral is a sum of positive differences (k+u)−2−(k+v)−2(k+u)^{-2}-(k+v)^{-2}, weighted by 00 or 11. With M=256M=256, the tail lies between (M+u)−1−(M+v)−1and(M+u)−1−(M+v)−1+(M+u)−2−(M+v)−2.(M+u)^{-1}-(M+v)^{-1} \quad\text{and}\quad (M+u)^{-1}-(M+v)^{-1}+(M+u)^{-2}-(M+v)^{-2}. This follows by comparing the positive decreasing summand with its integral. Outward rounding of rational numbers and Machin’s bounds for π\pi give, for each of the two maximisers, 0.40568302137302<C0/C1<0.40568302139506.0.40568302137302<C_0/C_1<0.40568302139506. Every other tuple has C0/C1<0.40563943278333C_0/C_1<0.40563943278333. The intervals therefore separate these two candidates from all other tuples, without relying on floating-point ordering.

Their exact equality is not inferred from overlapping intervals. Write ωA,ωB\omega_A,\omega_B for their step functions in the order just listed, and let JA,JBJ_A,J_B be their integrals against d(−ψ1)d(-\psi_1) on [0,1][0,1]. The floor formulas give ωB(u)−ωA(u)=⌊13u⌋+⌊15u⌋−2⌊14u⌋.\omega_B(u)-\omega_A(u) =\lfloor13u\rfloor+\lfloor15u\rfloor-2\lfloor14u\rfloor. For every positive integer cc, telescoping the cc intervals and splitting the defining trigamma series into residue classes gives ∫01⌊cu⌋d(−ψ1(u))=∑j=1c−1ψ1(j/c)−(c−1)ψ1(1)=c(c−1)π26.\int_0^1\lfloor cu\rfloor\,d(-\psi_1(u)) =\sum_{j=1}^{c-1}\psi_1(j/c)-(c-1)\psi_1(1) =\frac{c(c-1)\pi^2}{6}. Hence JB−JA=π2/3J_B-J_A=\pi^2/3. Both directions have m=15m=15 and C1=1091/2C_1=1091/2, while the quadratic part of C0C_0 before the 3/π23/\pi^2 correction is 266266 for AA and 265265 for BB. Its decrease by 11 exactly cancels the increase 3(JB−JA)/π2=13(J_B-J_A)/\pi^2=1. Thus C0C_0 also agrees.

A calculation compares every tuple of the box with interval bounds, and a second implementation repeats it with 512512 summands before the tail and a different enumeration order; both are in one program, with its recorded result. The calculation proves optimality only in the displayed finite box. No bound on a direction outside that box follows, and this calculation is not needed for the irrationality theorem.

The two-coordinate forms in 11 and F(p)F(p) should be distinguished from simultaneous approximation to two target values. Postelmans and Van Assche prove the ℚ\mathbb{Q}-linear independence of 1,ζq(1),ζq(2)1,\zeta_q(1),\zeta_q(2) for q=1/pq=1/p with integer p≥2p\ge2 [29]. Their confluent multiple little qq-Jacobi construction has two orthogonality conditions; its common integer normalisation and nonvanishing argument are in Section 6, especially (6.1)–(6.4). That theorem treats two target values and retains the integer inverse-base restriction. It supplies neither the coefficient pairs nor the all-base estimates assumed in Theorem 2.5; it is not an application at 3/23/2.

Finite calculations

This subsection separates exact checks from historical numerical reports. The polynomial reconstruction below covers n=1,2,3,4n=1,2,3,4, and the preceding parameter search has an exact comparison for every tuple in its finite box. Both exact checks are public, with the other finite calculations of this paper, in the reproduction guide, and a single script reruns them and compares each with its recorded result. The historical high-precision evaluations were not rerun. None of these finite calculations proves a statement for all indices, and none is a Lean proof. The rank-eight tests and the rational interval certificate are described separately.

The public reproduction guide gives the command and dependency pin for the direction-search program. Run it with --bound 30 and the output path named there; adding --check compares the result without replacing the stored search results. The stored record specifies mpmath 1.3.0 at thirty decimal digits. Its exact enumeration count is 37,53337{,}533, but its ordering by C0/C1C_0/C_1 is numerical and has no interval certificate in that historical record. The separate rational certificate above verifies the maximisers in the stated finite box; the archived program itself still uses numerical comparisons.

An exact integer calculation (program, every coefficient) reconstructs the forms of Section 2.1 directly in ℤ[X]\mathbb{Z}[X] from the displayed source formulas. It checks division by Ωn\Omega_n and XMnX^{M_n} with zero remainder and computes all coefficients of Un,VnU_n,V_n. A separate historical numerical report evaluated the remainder identity at those three bases to relative accuracy below 10−3910^{-39} at n=3n=3. It reported positivity of Λ̂n\widehat\Lambda_n and agreement with the bounds on HnH_n in Section 2.4. The historical constant evaluation used ω\omega, the thirteen intervals of Lemma 2.1 and forty-digit trigamma values. It reported J=77.94318447500909…,C0=221.30008816500502…,J=77.94318447500909\ldots,\qquad C_0=221.30008816500502\ldots, and C1/C0=2.46497868357497…C_1/C_0=2.46497868357497\ldots, agreeing with the source’s printed precision [8]. Power comparisons and Hankel determinants

The main Hankel calculation begins in Section 3.1 and uses none of the three numerical comparisons preceding it. Those comparisons give bounds for the later scalar and residue-count tests. The power bracket gives log⁡3/log⁡2<65/41\log3/\log2<65/41 and shows that 6565 is the least integer exponent qq for which 341<2q3^{41}<2^q. Failure of the rank-4141 selector count one row earlier uses the separate comparison 2129<3822^{129}<3^{82}. These comparisons settle the stated numerical inequalities, not the existence of the approximation families to which one might apply them.

The sharp qq-order of the normalised Hankel determinant

The preceding inequalities concern degrees used to clear denominators. We now determine a different quantity: the first nonzero term, as a formal power series in qq, of Zudilin’s normalised Hankel determinant at x=z=1x=z=1. Its order does not by itself give a divisor of an integer evaluation. That requires an integral normalisation and a separate divisibility proof. Zudilin builds the determinant by combining the Padé-type approximations of Bundschuh and Zudilin [11] with Bézivin’s method as developed in [12]; see [9]. His passage from the qq-order to the size of the determinant borrows the proofs of , as he notes in .

The source writes ℓp(x,z)=x∑r≥1zr/(pr−x)\ell_p(x,z)=x\sum_{r\ge1}z^r/(p^r-x), so ℓp(1,1)=F(p)\ell_p(1,1)=F(p). Here p=q−1p=q^{-1} and x,zx,z are auxiliary parameters, not the base. Write NN for the Hankel rank. With qq a formal variable, the moments and determinant in question are vm*=∑t≥0q(m+1)t(q;q)m3(qt+1;q)m(qm+t+1;q)m+1,VN*=det⁡(vi+j*)0≤i,j<N.v_m^*=\sum_{t\ge0}q^{(m+1)t} \frac{(q;q)_m^3(q^{t+1};q)_m}{(q^{m+t+1};q)_{m+1}}, \qquad V_N^*=\det(v_{i+j}^*)_{0\le i,j<N}. All product denominators have constant term 11, so their inverses exist in ℤ[[q]]\mathbb{Z}[[q]]. The order of a nonzero series is the least exponent of qq with a nonzero coefficient.

Theorem 3.4 (the first nonzero term at every rank). For every rank NN, the normalised Hankel determinant VN*V_N^{*} of [9], evaluated at x=z=1x=z=1, has ord⁡qVN*=N(N−1)(2N−1)6,leading coefficient(N!)2(N+1)!2N.\operatorname{ord}_q V_N^{*}=\frac{N(N-1)(2N-1)}{6}, \qquad \text{leading coefficient}\quad\frac{(N!)^{2}(N+1)!}{2^{N}} .

The source proves the order inequality and also gives |VN*(q)|≤|q|N3/3exp⁡(O(N2))|V_N^*(q)|\le |q|^{N^3/3}\exp(O(N^2)), referring to additional estimates for the passage from formal order to analytic size [9]. Equality in the order bound rules out a further initial power of qq at x=z=1x=z=1; it does not itself prove a fixed-qq estimate. For 0<q<10<q<1, the positive-measure argument below gives both positivity and a two-sided comparison with the leading term, with logarithmic error Oq(N)O_q(N). It refines the subleading control, not the cubic exponent of qq.

After pairing each positive-argument factor with one denominator, the ttth summand of GqG_q becomes wt(q;q)t(qt/2w;q)∞(w;q)∞(q(t+1)/2w;q)∞(w;q)∞×(−qt/2w;q)∞(−q(t+1)/2w;q)∞(w;q)∞(qtw;q)∞2.\begin{aligned} &\frac{w^t}{(q;q)_t} \frac{(q^{t/2}w;q)_\infty}{(w;q)_\infty} \frac{(q^{(t+1)/2}w;q)_\infty}{(w;q)_\infty}\\ &\qquad{}\times \frac{(-q^{t/2}w;q)_\infty(-q^{(t+1)/2}w;q)_\infty} {(w;q)_\infty(q^tw;q)_\infty^2}. \end{aligned} The qq-binomial identity makes the two ratios nonnegative coefficientwise; the remaining product also has nonnegative coefficients. When t=0t=0, the first ratio is 11 and every coefficient of the second is at least QQ. The last fraction has coefficients at least those of (1−w)−3(1-w)^{-3}. Thus the t=0t=0 term alone bounds γk\gamma_k below by Q(k+33)Q\binom{k+3}3.

For the upper bound, if RR has nonnegative coefficients and R(1)≤C<∞R(1)\le C<\infty, convolution with a nondecreasing sequence dkd_k is bounded by CdkCd_k. At t=0t=0, bound the second ratio coefficientwise by P−1(1−w)−1P^{-1}(1-w)^{-1}. After extracting (1−w)−3(1-w)^{-3} from the last fraction, its remaining factor has value at w=1w=1 at most TP−3TP^{-3}. This gives TP−4(k+33)TP^{-4}\binom{k+3}3. For t≥1t\ge1, both ratios are bounded by P−1(1−w)−1P^{-1}(1-w)^{-1}. Extracting the one factor (1−w)−1(1-w)^{-1} from the last fraction leaves a factor with value at 11 at most TP−3TP^{-3}; also (q;q)t−1≤P−1(q;q)_t^{-1}\le P^{-1}. The ttth summand is therefore bounded coefficientwise by TP−6wt(1−w)−3TP^{-6}w^t(1-w)^{-3}. Summing t≥1t\ge1 gives TP−6(k+23)TP^{-6}\binom{k+2}3 as the bound for its kkth coefficient. Consequently Q3ck≤γk≤T(P−4+P−6)ck.\frac Q3 c_k\le\gamma_k\le T(P^{-4}+P^{-6})c_k. Thus ∑k≥0P4γkqkδqk\sum_{k\ge0}P^4\gamma_kq^k\delta_{q^k} is a finite positive measure on [0,1][0,1], with infinitely many distinct support points and moments vm*(q)v_m^*(q). In standard terminology, (vm*(q))m≥0(v_m^*(q))_{m\ge0} is a Hausdorff moment sequence. This statement fixes qq; the measure is not a representing measure for the coefficient sequence sm(p)s_m(p) considered in the next subsection. A nonzero polynomial of degree less than NN cannot vanish at all of its first NN atoms; the associated Gram matrix is positive definite. Truncate the measure to its first K+1K+1 atoms. At fixed rank NN, each matrix entry converges as K→∞K\to\infty, and the determinant converges because it is a polynomial in those entries. Finite Cauchy–Binet and monotone convergence of the nonnegative tuple sums therefore give Heine’s expansion, whose integral form is reproved in [10]: VN*=∑k0<⋯<kN−1∏i(P4γkiqki)∏i<j(qki−qkj)2.V_N^*=\sum_{k_0<\cdots<k_{N-1}} \prod_i(P^4\gamma_{k_i}q^{k_i})\prod_{i<j}(q^{k_i}-q^{k_j})^2. Retaining the tuple ki=ik_i=i and using ∏d=1N−1(1−qd)2(N−d)≥P2N\prod_{d=1}^{N-1}(1-q^d)^{2(N-d)}\ge P^{2N} gives the lower bound below. For the upper bound put ki=i+λik_i=i+\lambda_i, where the λi\lambda_i are nonnegative and nondecreasing. Factoring the smaller power from each Vandermonde difference gives the exact exponent ∑iki+2∑i<jki=BN+∑i=0N−1(2N−1−2i)λi.\sum_i k_i+2\sum_{i<j}k_i =B_N+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}(2N-1-2i)\lambda_i. Every weight 2N−1−2i2N-1-2i is at least 11. Since 0<q<10<q<1, the remaining power of qq is at most q∑iλiq^{\sum_i\lambda_i}. Also ci+λ/ci≤(λ+1)3c_{i+\lambda}/c_i\le(\lambda+1)^3. Discard the remaining Vandermonde factors, each bounded by 11, and enlarge the nonnegative sum by dropping the ordering restriction on the λi\lambda_i. It now factors into NN copies of ∑λ≥0(λ+1)3qλ\sum_{\lambda\ge0}(\lambda+1)^3q^\lambda, which gives (P6Q/3)NCNqBN≤VN*(q)≤[P4T(P−4+P−6)1+4q+q2(1−q)4]NCNqBN.(P^6Q/3)^N C_Nq^{B_N}\le V_N^*(q) \le\left[P^4T(P^{-4}+P^{-6}) \frac{1+4q+q^2}{(1-q)^4}\right]^N C_Nq^{B_N}. Both constants are positive and finite, so VN*(q)>0V_N^*(q)>0 and log⁡(VN*(q)/(CNqBN))=Oq(N)\log(V_N^*(q)/(C_Nq^{B_N}))=O_q(N), including N=0N=0 under the empty determinant convention. Here N→∞N\to\infty with qq fixed; the constants are not uniform as q↑1q\uparrow1. The formal-order calculation instead fixes NN and expands at q=0q=0. No joint uniform limit is asserted. The measure depends on qq, not on the moment index or rank, and supplies no denominator factor for the 2004 polynomial forms. Section 3.2 replaces the band Oq(N)O_q(N) by an exact asymptotic with an explicit positive constant, using the same weights.

Formal verification and computations.

The positive-measure argument, including its generating-function identification and infinite determinant expansion, is an ordinary proof and is not formalised. The formal-series argument has a checked recurrence for the leading coefficients. The Lean proof of Theorem 3.4 uses the first nonzero term of every transformed row, which for row 11 has order exactly l+1l+1 and coefficient exactly −6-6 in every column. Independently of the proof, the order and the leading coefficient were computed exactly for 1≤N≤71\le N\le7 (program, result), giving orders 0,1,5,14,30,55,910,1,5,14,30,55,91 and leading coefficients 1,6,108,4320,324000,40824000,80015040001,6,108,4320,324000,40824000,8001504000, each matching the closed forms.

Earlier work and the unresolved value at 3/23/2.

The antecedent is the inequality of [9]; the equality and the leading coefficient are proved here. Lemma 3.5 and [long1049:eq:row-initial] give that row calculation. Nothing in this subsection decides the arithmetic nature of F(3/2)F(3/2).

The size of VN*V_N^* at a fixed base

The positive-measure argument traps log⁡(VN*(q)/(CNqBN))\log(V_N^*(q)/(C_Nq^{B_N})) between two multiples of NN. It leaves the exponential rate inside that band undetermined, and says nothing about the correction below it. Both are determined here. Throughout this subsection 0<q<10<q<1 is fixed and P=(q;q)∞,ℳ(q)=∏d≥1(1−qd)−d,L=F(1/q)=∑r≥1qr1−qr,P=(q;q)_\infty,\qquad \mathcal M(q)=\prod_{d\ge1}(1-q^d)^{-d},\qquad L=F(1/q)=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{q^r}{1-q^r}, with BN=∑j<Nj2B_N=\sum_{j<N}j^2 and CN=∏k<Nck=(N!)2(N+1)!/2NC_N=\prod_{k<N}c_k=(N!)^2(N+1)!/2^N as above. Both products converge to positive finite values, and the abbreviation LL is used only in this subsection; it is the value at qq of the divisor series ℒ\mathcal L of Section 10. Nothing in this subsection changes a denominator valuation or supplies a divisor for the 2004 polynomial forms.

The first step isolates what a Hankel determinant needs from its weights. The hypotheses are two ratio conditions on the weights, so the theorem covers other moment families of the same geometric shape as well.

Theorem 3.6 (determinants of geometric moments). Let ak>0a_k>0 satisfy, for fixed constants CC and κ\kappa, ak+hak→1(k→∞) for each fixed h≥0,ak+hak≤C(1+h)κ(k,h≥0).\frac{a_{k+h}}{a_k}\longrightarrow1\quad(k\to\infty) \text{ for each fixed }h\ge0, \qquad \frac{a_{k+h}}{a_k}\le C(1+h)^\kappa\quad(k,h\ge0). Put Mm=∑k≥0akq(m+1)kM_m=\sum_{k\ge0}a_kq^{(m+1)k} and DN=det⁡(Mi+j)0≤i,j<ND_N=\det(M_{i+j})_{0\le i,j<N}. Then DN∼ℳ(q)3qBNP2N∏k=0N−1ak(N→∞).D_N\sim\mathcal M(q)^3\,q^{B_N}P^{2N}\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}a_k \qquad(N\to\infty).

Proof. Taking k=0k=0 in the ratio bound gives ah≤Ca0(1+h)κa_h\le Ca_0(1+h)^\kappa, so every moment converges. Heine’s expansion, as in Section 3, writes DN=∑k0<⋯<kN−1∏i<N(akiqki)∏i<j<N(qki−qkj)2,D_N=\sum_{k_0<\cdots<k_{N-1}} \prod_{i<N}\bigl(a_{k_i}q^{k_i}\bigr) \prod_{i<j<N}(q^{k_i}-q^{k_j})^2, a sum of positive terms. Write ki=i+λik_i=i+\lambda_i with 0≤λ0≤⋯≤λN−10\le\lambda_0\le\cdots\le\lambda_{N-1}. The tuple λ=0\lambda=0 contributes qBN∏i<Nai⋅ΔN,ΔN=∏d=1N−1(1−qd)2(N−d).q^{B_N}\prod_{i<N}a_i\cdot\Delta_N, \qquad \Delta_N=\prod_{d=1}^{N-1}(1-q^d)^{2(N-d)}. Reverse the shifts by setting μj=λN−j\mu_j=\lambda_{N-j} for 1≤j≤N1\le j\le N, so that μ1≥μ2≥⋯≥μN≥0\mu_1\ge\mu_2\ge\cdots\ge\mu_N\ge0 is a partition. Dividing the general summand by the displayed contribution leaves WN(μ)=q∑j≤N(2j−1)μj∏j≤NaN−j+μjaN−j∏1≤j<k≤N(1−qk−j+μj−μk1−qk−j)2,W_N(\mu)= q^{\sum_{j\le N}(2j-1)\mu_j} \prod_{j\le N}\frac{a_{N-j+\mu_j}}{a_{N-j}} \prod_{1\le j<k\le N} \left(\frac{1-q^{k-j+\mu_j-\mu_k}}{1-q^{k-j}}\right)^2, because the summand indexed by (ki)(k_i) has qq-exponent BN+∑i(2N−1−2i)λiB_N+\sum_i(2N-1-2i)\lambda_i and the weight 2N−1−2i2N-1-2i becomes 2j−12j-1 under i=N−ji=N-j. Thus DN/(qBNΔN∏i<Nai)=∑μWN(μ)D_N/(q^{B_N}\Delta_N\prod_{i<N}a_i)=\sum_\mu W_N(\mu).

Let ℓ\ell be the length of μ\mu, that is, the number of positive parts. Only the indices j≤ℓj\le\ell contribute a ratio different from 11. For fixed j≤ℓj\le\ell the partition is decreasing, so k−j+μj−μk≥k−jk-j+\mu_j-\mu_k\ge k-j for every k>jk>j; the numerators are at most 11 and the denominators multiply to at least PP. Each of the ℓ\ell squared factors is therefore at most P−2P^{-2}, and the weight ratios contribute at most ∏j≤ℓC(1+μj)κ\prod_{j\le\ell}C(1+\mu_j)^\kappa. Hence WN(μ)≤(CP−2)ℓ∏j=1ℓ(1+μj)κq(2j−1)μjfor every N.W_N(\mu)\le(CP^{-2})^{\ell} \prod_{j=1}^{\ell}(1+\mu_j)^\kappa q^{(2j-1)\mu_j} \qquad\text{for every }N. Summing this majorant over all partitions of length exactly ℓ\ell, after dropping the ordering constraint on the positive parts, factorises it into (CP−2)ℓ∏j=1ℓ∑u≥1(1+u)κq(2j−1)u≤Cqℓqℓ2,Cq=CP−2∑u≥1(1+u)κqu−1,(CP^{-2})^{\ell}\prod_{j=1}^{\ell} \sum_{u\ge1}(1+u)^\kappa q^{(2j-1)u} \le C_q^{\ell}q^{\ell^2}, \qquad C_q=CP^{-2}\sum_{u\ge1}(1+u)^\kappa q^{u-1}, using q(2j−1)u≤q2j−1qu−1q^{(2j-1)u}\le q^{2j-1}q^{u-1} and ∑j≤ℓ(2j−1)=ℓ2\sum_{j\le\ell}(2j-1)=\ell^2. The resulting bound is summable in ℓ\ell, and it does not depend on NN.

For each fixed partition μ\mu, the weight ratios tend to 11 as N→∞N\to\infty by the first hypothesis, and the Vandermonde quotient converges to the corresponding infinite product. The limit of WN(μ)W_N(\mu) is therefore the same function of μ\mu that the weights ak≡1a_k\equiv1 produce, since those weights give ratio 11 identically and leave the Vandermonde quotient unchanged. Dominated convergence over partitions now identifies lim⁡N∑μWN(μ)\lim_N\sum_\mu W_N(\mu) with the corresponding limit in the unit-weight case.

For ak≡1a_k\equiv1 the moments are Mm=(1−qm+1)−1M_m=(1-q^{m+1})^{-1}, and Cauchy’s determinant evaluates DN=qBNΔN∏0≤i,j<N(1−qi+j+1).D_N=\frac{q^{B_N}\Delta_N}{\prod_{0\le i,j<N}(1-q^{i+j+1})}. The exponent of 1−qm1-q^m in that denominator is min⁡(m,N,2N−m)\min(m,N,2N-m), which increases to mm, so the denominator tends to ℳ(q)−1\mathcal M(q)^{-1} and the quotient ∑μWN(μ)\sum_\mu W_N(\mu) tends to ℳ(q)\mathcal M(q). Finally ΔNP2N=∏d<N(1−qd)−2d∏d≥N(1−qd)−2N→ℳ(q)2,\frac{\Delta_N}{P^{2N}} =\prod_{d<N}(1-q^d)^{-2d}\prod_{d\ge N}(1-q^d)^{-2N} \longrightarrow\mathcal M(q)^2, because the logarithm of the second product is Oq(NqN)O_q(Nq^N). Multiplying the two limits proves the theorem. ◻

The hypotheses hold for the actual weights ak=P4γka_k=P^4\gamma_k, and the reason is an exact algebraic identity. It also sharpens the comparison (Q/3)ck≤γk≤T(P−4+P−6)ck(Q/3)c_k\le\gamma_k\le T(P^{-4}+P^{-6})c_k of the previous subsection to two explicit powers of PP.

Proposition 3.7 (the moment weights as a product of two finite sums). For r≥1r\ge1 and k≥0k\ge0 set Rk(r)(q)=∑n1+⋯+nr=k(q;q)k∏j≤r(q;q)nj,R_k^{(r)}(q)=\sum_{n_1+\cdots+n_r=k} \frac{(q;q)_k}{\prod_{j\le r}(q;q)_{n_j}}, the sum being over compositions into rr nonnegative parts, so that Rk(r)R_k^{(r)} is the sum of all qq-multinomial coefficients of degree kk and length rr, equivalently the multivariate Rogers–Szegő polynomial at unit arguments [40]. These are polynomial identities in the indeterminate qq; at a prime power, r=2r=2 gives the Galois number counting the subspaces of a kk-dimensional space over the field of that order, and r=3r=3 counts the flags V1⊆V2V_1\subseteq V_2 in that space. The source is cited for those identifications; the factorisation below is proved here. Then γk(q)=Rk(2)(q)Rk(3)(q)(q;q)k.\gamma_k(q)=\frac{R_k^{(2)}(q)R_k^{(3)}(q)}{(q;q)_k}. The product Rk(2)Rk(3)R_k^{(2)}R_k^{(3)} lies in ℤ≥0[q]\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}[q], has degree ⌊k2/4⌋+⌊k2/3⌋\lfloor k^2/4\rfloor+\lfloor k^2/3\rfloor, and has coefficient sum 6k6^k. Consequently (q;q)kγk∈ℤ[q](q;q)_k\gamma_k\in\mathbb{Z}[q], and the weights ak=P4γka_k=P^4\gamma_k satisfy P5ck≤ak≤P−1ck(k≥0),P^5c_k\le a_k\le P^{-1}c_k \qquad(k\ge0), together with ak+h/ak≤P−6(1+h)3a_{k+h}/a_k\le P^{-6}(1+h)^3, so the hypotheses of Theorem 3.6 hold with κ=3\kappa=3.

Proof. Write ℰ(z)=(z;q)∞−1\mathcal E(z)=(z;q)_\infty^{-1} and ∂qf(z)=(f(z)−f(qz))/z\partial_qf(z)=(f(z)-f(qz))/z, so that ∂qℰ=ℰ\partial_q\mathcal E=\mathcal E and ℰ(z)r=∑n≥0Rn(r)zn/(q;q)n\mathcal E(z)^r=\sum_{n\ge0}R_n^{(r)}z^n/(q;q)_n by Euler’s expansion. The qq-Leibniz rule, which follows by induction from the product rule, is ∂qn(fg)(z)=∑j=0n[nj]q(∂qjf)(qn−jz)(∂qn−jg)(z).\partial_q^n(fg)(z)=\sum_{j=0}^n\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{n}{j}_q (\partial_q^jf)(q^{n-j}z)\,(\partial_q^{n-j}g)(z). Write hk(z)=∑j=0k[kj]q(z;q)jh_k(z)=\sum_{j=0}^k\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{k}{j}_q(z;q)_j. Applying it once more, to ℰ⋅ℰ2\mathcal E\cdot\mathcal E^2, gives ∂qnℰ(z)3=ℰ(z)3∑k=0n[nk]q(z;q)khk(z),\partial_q^n\mathcal E(z)^3 =\mathcal E(z)^3\sum_{k=0}^n\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{n}{k}_q(z;q)_kh_k(z), the power of ℰ\mathcal E being 33 and not 22 here. Hence ∑n≥0wn(q;q)n∂qnℰ(z)3=ℰ(w)ℰ(z)3∑k≥0wk(z;q)k(q;q)khk(z).\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{w^n}{(q;q)_n}\partial_q^n\mathcal E(z)^3 =\mathcal E(w)\mathcal E(z)^3 \sum_{k\ge0}\frac{w^k(z;q)_k}{(q;q)_k}h_k(z). Put z=wz=w. On the left the coefficient of wnw^n is Rn(3)∑j≤n((q;q)j(q;q)n−j)−1=Rn(2)Rn(3)/(q;q)nR_n^{(3)}\sum_{j\le n}\bigl((q;q)_j(q;q)_{n-j}\bigr)^{-1} =R_n^{(2)}R_n^{(3)}/(q;q)_n. On the right, expand hkh_k and set k=j+tk=j+t; the inner sum is evaluated by the qq-binomial theorem as ∑t≥0(wqj;q)t(q;q)twt=(w2qj;q)∞(w;q)∞,\sum_{t\ge0}\frac{(wq^j;q)_t}{(q;q)_t}w^t =\frac{(w^2q^j;q)_\infty}{(w;q)_\infty}, and the result is exactly Gq(w)G_q(w). Every step holds coefficientwise, and absolutely for |w||w| small.

A qq-multinomial coefficient has nonnegative integral coefficients, degree ∑i<jninj\sum_{i<j}n_in_j, and value 11 at q=1q=1 after division by the corresponding multinomial. Summing over compositions gives coefficient sum rkr^k for Rk(r)R_k^{(r)} and hence 6k6^k for the product. The degree is maximised by balanced parts, which gives ⌊k2/4⌋\lfloor k^2/4\rfloor for r=2r=2 and ⌊k2/3⌋\lfloor k^2/3\rfloor for r=3r=3; no leading cancellation occurs because all coefficients are nonnegative.

For the bounds, write bk(r)=[zk](z;q)∞−rb_k^{(r)}=[z^k](z;q)_\infty^{-r}, so that Rk(r)=(q;q)kbk(r)R_k^{(r)}=(q;q)_kb_k^{(r)} and γk=(q;q)kbk(2)bk(3)\gamma_k=(q;q)_kb_k^{(2)}b_k^{(3)}. Euler’s expansion exhibits bk(r)b_k^{(r)} as an rr-fold convolution of the sequence 1/(q;q)n1/(q;q)_n, whose terms lie in [1,P−1][1,P^{-1}]; the number of compositions of kk into rr nonnegative parts is (k+r−1r−1)\binom{k+r-1}{r-1}, so (k+r−1r−1)≤bk(r)≤P−r(k+r−1r−1).\binom{k+r-1}{r-1}\le b_k^{(r)}\le P^{-r}\binom{k+r-1}{r-1}. Combining these at r=2,3r=2,3 with P≤(q;q)k≤1P\le(q;q)_k\le1 and ck=(k+1)(k+22)c_k=(k+1)\binom{k+2}2 gives P5ck≤ak≤P−1ckP^5c_k\le a_k\le P^{-1}c_k. The shift bound follows from ck+h/ck≤(1+h)3c_{k+h}/c_k\le(1+h)^3.

It remains to show that ak+h/ak→1a_{k+h}/a_k\to1 for each fixed hh. Put en=1/(q;q)ne_n=1/(q;q)_n. Since (q;q)n+1=(1−qn+1)(q;q)n(q;q)_{n+1}=(1-q^{n+1})(q;q)_n, these terms satisfy 1=e0≤e1≤⋯≤P−11=e_0\le e_1\le\cdots\le P^{-1}, and the convolutions read bk(2)=∑i≤keiek−ib_k^{(2)}=\sum_{i\le k}e_ie_{k-i} and bk(3)=∑i≤keibk−i(2)b_k^{(3)}=\sum_{i\le k}e_ib_{k-i}^{(2)}. Hence bk+1(2)−bk(2)=∑i≤kei(ek+1−i−ek−i)+ek+1,bk+1(3)−bk(3)=∑i≤kei(bk+1−i(2)−bk−i(2))+ek+1.\begin{aligned} b_{k+1}^{(2)}-b_k^{(2)} &=\sum_{i\le k}e_i\bigl(e_{k+1-i}-e_{k-i}\bigr)+e_{k+1},\\ b_{k+1}^{(3)}-b_k^{(3)} &=\sum_{i\le k}e_i\bigl(b_{k+1-i}^{(2)}-b_{k-i}^{(2)}\bigr)+e_{k+1}. \end{aligned} Every bracket is nonnegative. In the first line the brackets add up to ek+1−1<P−1e_{k+1}-1<P^{-1} and each ei≤P−1e_i\le P^{-1}, so 0≤bk+1(2)−bk(2)≤P−2+P−1≤2P−20\le b_{k+1}^{(2)}-b_k^{(2)}\le P^{-2}+P^{-1}\le2P^{-2}. Inserting this bound into the k+1k+1 terms of the second line gives 0≤bk+1(3)−bk(3)≤2(k+1)P−3+P−1≤3(k+1)P−30\le b_{k+1}^{(3)}-b_k^{(3)}\le2(k+1)P^{-3}+P^{-1}\le3(k+1)P^{-3}. Against the lower bounds bk(2)≥k+1b_k^{(2)}\ge k+1 and bk(3)≥(k+1)(k+2)/2b_k^{(3)}\ge(k+1)(k+2)/2 displayed above, the ratio bk+1(r)/bk(r)b_{k+1}^{(r)}/b_k^{(r)} lies in [1,1+2P−2/(k+1)][1,1+2P^{-2}/(k+1)] for r=2r=2 and in [1,1+6P−3/(k+2)][1,1+6P^{-3}/(k+2)] for r=3r=3. Both ratios tend to 11, and therefore so does bk+h(r)/bk(r)b_{k+h}^{(r)}/b_k^{(r)}, a product of hh consecutive ratios. Finally (q;q)k+h/(q;q)k=∏j=1h(1−qk+j)→1(q;q)_{k+h}/(q;q)_k=\prod_{j=1}^h(1-q^{k+j})\to1, and ak+h/ak=γk+h/γka_{k+h}/a_k=\gamma_{k+h}/\gamma_k is the product of these three ratios. Only one analytic input is still missing, namely the behaviour of ak/cka_k/c_k to second order. It is supplied by the two leading coefficients of GqG_q at its singularity w=1w=1.

What the sharp estimate settles, and what it leaves.

The positive-measure argument of the previous subsection had recorded this shape as a candidate without its constant. The proof, the limiting Gram factor ℳ(q)3\mathcal M(q)^3 and the convergent expression for the constant are supplied here. The estimate replaces the band Oq(N)O_q(N) by the explicit terms 2Nlog⁡P2N\log P, −8F(1/q)log⁡N-8F(1/q)\log N and the constant log⁡K(q)\log K(q), with an o(1)o(1) error, and the weights now have an exact finite description rather than an infinite-product representation alone.

The cubic exponent of qq is untouched, and so is every prime-power valuation. At 3/23/2 the deficit is unchanged and is exactly 3941(4N3−3N2)−(2N3−N)=N(74N2−117N+41)41>0(N≥2),\frac{39}{41}\bigl(4N^3-3N^2\bigr)-\bigl(2N^3-N\bigr) =\frac{N(74N^2-117N+41)}{41}>0\qquad(N\ge2), the positivity being immediate from 74N2−117N+41=74(N−2)2+179(N−2)+10374N^2-117N+41=74(N-2)^2+179(N-2)+103. Its leading size is (74/41)N3(74/41)N^3, so no estimate that leaves the cubic coefficient alone can close it. The finite factorisation describes the same weights in a new way; it does not license substituting their denominator for the denominator of a cleared linear form.

A positive expansion is not a moment representation.

Substituting x=pm+1x=p^{m+1} into Van Assche’s alternative expansion [17] gives the identity Rm(p)=∑k=0m[mk]p[m+kk]pp(m−k)(m−k+1)/2∏j=m−k+1m(pj−1).R_m(p)=\sum_{k=0}^m\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{m}{k}_p\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{m+k}{k}_p p^{(m-k)(m-k+1)/2}\prod_{j=m-k+1}^{m}(p^j-1). Indeed (qx;q)k=(−1)k∏j=m−k+1m(pj−1)(qx;q)_k=(-1)^k\prod_{j=m-k+1}^m(p^j-1), so the two signs cancel. This proves Rm(p)>0R_m(p)>0 for p>1p>1, and nonnegative coefficients in the variable t=p−1t=p-1; it does not prove Hankel positivity. In fact, det⁡(Ri+j(p))i,j<3=−36(p−1)2+O((p−1)3)(p↓1).\det(R_{i+j}(p))_{i,j<3}=-36(p-1)^2+O((p-1)^3) \quad(p\downarrow1). A geometric factor cρmc\rho^m with c,ρ>0c,\rho>0 would change a Hankel matrix only by a positive scalar and an invertible diagonal congruence, so it would preserve positive definiteness. The factor ([m]p!)3([m]_p!)^3 is not geometric: its values at m=0,1,2m=0,1,2 are 1,1,(1+p)31,1,(1+p)^3. It cannot be discarded in testing the moment condition. Nor does its positivity alone prove that multiplication by it repairs the failed condition for RmR_m. At p=1p=1, sm(1)=(m!)3s_m(1)=(m!)^3 is the moment sequence of a product of three independent unit exponential variables, since their mmth moments multiply. This is only the polynomial endpoint; F(1)F(1) diverges. Berg’s Theorem 5.1 states that (m!)c(m!)^c is Stieltjes indeterminate for c>2c>2 [34]. Thus a measure exists at the endpoint but is not unique. Neither uniqueness nor a canonical deformation is a premise of the question at p>1p>1.

Finite certificates and an all-rank degree check.

For the eight unshifted determinants, positivity is also a Lean theorem, proved by a different certificate. Put T=22929T=2^{2929}. The degrees admit a separate all-rank proof. The Gaussian binomial [uv]p\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{u}{v}_p is monic of degree v(u−v)v(u-v). In the signed sum for RmR_m, the degree increases by 2m−k2m-k from the kkth to the (k+1)(k+1)st term. The unique maximal term is k=mk=m, with positive leading coefficient. Hence RmR_m is monic of degree (3m2+m)/2(3m^2+m)/2, and sms_m is monic of degree 3m2−m3m^2-m. In the determinant, the only permutation-dependent part of the degree is 6∑iiσ(i)6\sum_i i\sigma(i); strict rearrangement makes the identity its unique maximum. Therefore deg⁡DN,h=∑i=0N−1(3(2i+h)2−(2i+h)),lc⁡DN,h=1.\deg D_{N,h}=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\bigl(3(2i+h)^2-(2i+h)\bigr), \qquad \operatorname{lc}D_{N,h}=1. More generally the same argument works for a fixed minor with distinct increasing row and column indices. Each such minor is positive for all sufficiently large pp, with a threshold that may depend on the minor. At p=1p=1, both leading Hankel families are positive definite by the infinite-support product measure, so each fixed rank is also positive in some neighbourhood of 11. Neither argument provides a neighbourhood or large-base threshold uniform over every rank.

A Stieltjes moment representation requires positive semidefiniteness of both Hankel families at all ranks. The positive-definite formulation for nondegenerate sequences is stated in [31]; finite support requires allowing semidefinite matrices. The necessity of both conditions is visible from their quadratic forms: if a positive measure μ\mu on [0,∞)[0,\infty) satisfies sm=∫0∞xmdμ(x)s_m=\int_0^\infty x^m\,d\mu(x), and P(x)=∑i=0N−1cixiP(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}c_ix^i has real coefficients, then ∑i,j=0N−1cicjsi+j+h=∫0∞xhP(x)2dμ(x)≥0,h=0,1.\sum_{i,j=0}^{N-1}c_ic_j s_{i+j+h} =\int_0^\infty x^hP(x)^2\,d\mu(x)\ge0, \qquad h=0,1. The shifted test records nonnegative support, not merely positivity of the measure. For example, the positive point mass at −1-1 has moments (−1)m(-1)^m. Its unshifted quadratic form is P(−1)2P(-1)^2, whereas its shifted form is −P(−1)2-P(-1)^2. Thus a Hamburger moment sequence, which permits support anywhere on ℝ\mathbb{R}, need not be a Stieltjes moment sequence. The two tests above do not assert a measure for the entire coefficient sequence considered here. Coefficientwise total positivity would be stronger than the sixteen certificates above. Positive production matrices and path constructions can supply such a mechanism in other families [36][37]; no such matrix for this moving-degree sequence has been established here.

A finite spectral consequence.

Write AN=(αi+j)0≤i,j<NA_N=(\alpha_{i+j})_{0\le i,j<N} and BN=(βi+j)0≤i,j<NB_N=(\beta_{i+j})_{0\le i,j<N}. Let D=diag⁡(1,p(p−1)3,…,[p(p−1)3]N−1)D=\operatorname{diag}(1,p(p-1)^3,\ldots,[p(p-1)^3]^{N-1}). Then AN=pD(si+j)DA_N=pD(s_{i+j})D. For p>1p>1 this is an invertible positive diagonal congruence. The remainder representation already proves F(p)AN−BN=(vi+j*)>0F(p)A_N-B_N=(v^*_{i+j})>0 at every rank.

Proposition 3.9 (finite coefficient positivity and pencil roots). For every real p>1p>1 and 1≤N≤81\le N\le8, ANA_N is positive definite and all roots of det⁡(YAN−BN)\det(YA_N-B_N) are real and strictly less than F(p)F(p). The roots at consecutive ranks N,N+1≤8N,N+1\le8 interlace non-strictly.

Proof. The leading principal minors of (si+j)i,j<N(s_{i+j})_{i,j<N} are exactly Dk,0(p)D_{k,0}(p) for 1≤k≤N1\le k\le N; their coefficient positivity proved above, together with Sylvester’s criterion, gives positive definiteness. The diagonal congruence gives AN>0A_N>0. The real symmetric matrix AN−1/2BNAN−1/2A_N^{-1/2}B_NA_N^{-1/2} has these pencil roots as eigenvalues, and F(p)I−AN−1/2BNAN−1/2>0F(p)I-A_N^{-1/2}B_NA_N^{-1/2}>0 puts them strictly below F(p)F(p). The minimum–maximum principle for x𝖳BNx/(x𝖳ANx)x^{\mathsf T}B_Nx/(x^{\mathsf T}A_Nx) on nested coordinate subspaces gives non-strict interlacing. These are subspaces for the original pencils; the separately conjugated symmetric matrices need not be principal submatrices of one another. ◻

Proposition 3.9 uses only the eight unshifted certificates Dk,0D_{k,0}, not an all-rank coefficient measure. The shifted certificates Dk,1D_{k,1} are used below for a truncated Stieltjes moment representation and the first fifteen continued-fraction coefficients, not for this application of Sylvester’s criterion. An infinite-support coefficient measure would extend the pencil argument to all ranks. At the certified ranks, the largest root is a nondecreasing lower bound for F(p)F(p); convergence to F(p)F(p), simple roots, strict interlacing and denominator control are not established. At p=1p=1 the congruence degenerates and FF diverges, so the proposition excludes that endpoint.

The pencil is different from the Jacobi matrix of the coefficient moments. This is already visible at rank two. The defining formulas give β0=0,β1=p3(p−1)2(p+2)>0(p>1).\beta_0=0,\qquad \beta_1=p^3(p-1)^2(p+2)>0\quad(p>1). Consequently det⁡B2=−β12<0\det B_2=-\beta_1^2<0. Since A2>0A_2>0, the product of the two real pencil roots is det⁡B2/det⁡A2<0\det B_2/\det A_2<0: one root is negative and the other positive. In contrast, the finite Stieltjes construction below has only positive nodes. Positivity of the coefficient Hankel matrix therefore does not identify these two spectral constructions.

Formal continued fractions and finite quadrature.

Write Dn=Dn,0D_n=D_{n,0}, En=Dn,1E_n=D_{n,1}, with D0=E0=1D_0=E_0=1. All these determinant polynomials are nonzero by the all-rank degree calculation above. Here s0=1s_0=1, and the identity is in ℚ(p)[[z]]\mathbb{Q}(p)[[z]]. The classical moment correspondence is recalled in . Specialising a ratio at a fixed real pp requires its displayed denominators to be nonzero. The sixteen certificates ensure this and λ1,…,λ15>0\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{15}>0 for every p≥1p\ge1; they do not ensure it at all indices. Seeking positive formulas for all these ratios is therefore a specific version of the coefficient-moment question. The generating series has radius of convergence zero for every p≥1p\ge1, so the displayed identity must be read formally. At p=1p=1 this follows from sm(1)=(m!)3s_m(1)=(m!)^3. For p>1p>1, the k=0k=0 term of the positive expansion for RmR_m and the inequality [m]p!≥pm(m−1)/2[m]_p!\ge p^{m(m-1)/2} give sm(p)≥p2m2−m.s_m(p)\ge p^{2m^2-m}. Thus sm(p)1/m→∞s_m(p)^{1/m}\to\infty. This concerns the moment power series; it does not decide convergence of the continued fraction at an individual nonzero value of zz.

For each fixed p≥1p\ge1, the two positive 8×88\times8 moment matrices give a positive measure with eight atoms representing s0,…,s15s_0,\ldots,s_{15}. This can be proved without assuming an infinite representing measure. Set H0=(si+j)i,j<8,H1=(si+j+1)i,j<8,T=H0−1H1,H_0=(s_{i+j})_{i,j<8},\qquad H_1=(s_{i+j+1})_{i,j<8},\qquad T=H_0^{-1}H_1, and give ℝ8\mathbb{R}^8 the inner product ⟨u,v⟩=u𝖳H0v\langle u,v\rangle=u^{\mathsf T}H_0v. The operator TT is self-adjoint and positive definite because H0T=H1H_0T=H_1 is symmetric and positive definite. If e0,…,e7e_0,\ldots,e_7 are the coordinate vectors, the Hankel identities give Tej=ej+1Te_j=e_{j+1} for 0≤j<70\le j<7. Hence e0e_0 is cyclic: its first eight iterates form a basis. The spectral theorem now gives eight distinct positive eigenvalues and a positive weight at each, namely the squared norm of the corresponding projection of e0e_0. Cyclicity ensures that no projection vanishes and that no eigenspace has dimension greater than one.

Let ν\nu be the resulting atomic measure. For 0≤m≤140\le m\le14, choose i,j≤7i,j\le7 with i+j=mi+j=m. Self-adjointness gives ∫xmdν(x)=⟨Tme0,e0⟩=⟨ei,ej⟩=sm.\int x^m\,d\nu(x)=\langle T^m e_0,e_0\rangle =\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=s_m. For the last moment, ∫x15dν(x)=⟨T7e0,TT7e0⟩=e7𝖳H1e7=s15.\int x^{15}\,d\nu(x)=\langle T^7e_0,T T^7e_0\rangle =e_7^{\mathsf T}H_1e_7=s_{15}. The weights sum to s0=1s_0=1. Hence the measure agrees with the moment functional on every polynomial of degree at most 1515; this is the degree range certified for the eight-node quadrature obtained here. In an orthonormal polynomial basis it is the classical Jacobi construction; Golub and Welsch describe the computation of its nodes and weights [39]. Nothing here identifies the subsequent moments of ν\nu with s16,s17,…s_{16},s_{17},\ldots. This finite construction must also be distinguished from the coefficient pencil (AN,BN)(A_N,B_N). For rational modifications of an already known moment functional, see Krattenthaler [30]; such a modification producing the entire sequence sms_m has not been identified.

Testing for additional cyclotomic factors.

Independently of the moment question, let vΦdv_{\Phi_d} denote the multiplicity of the cyclotomic factor Φd\Phi_d in a nonzero polynomial in ℚ[p]\mathbb{Q}[p], and set vΦd(0)=∞v_{\Phi_d}(0)=\infty. For a 2×22\times2 matrix with entry valuations 0,2,2,50,2,2,5, the two determinant products have valuations 55 and 44. The lower one is unique, so the determinant has valuation 44. A tie is different: all four entries of (1111+Φd)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&1+\Phi_d\end{smallmatrix}\right) have valuation zero, but its determinant is Φd\Phi_d. At general rank, we must find the least total valuation and then test whether the terms attaining it cancel. For N,d≥1N,d\ge1, define ℋN(Y;p)=det⁡(αi+jY−βi+j)i,j<N,tm,d=min⁡(vΦd(αm),vΦd(βm)),eN,d=minσ∈SN∑i=0N−1ti+σ(i),d.\begin{aligned} \mathcal H_N(Y;p)&=\det(\alpha_{i+j}Y-\beta_{i+j})_{i,j<N},\\ t_{m,d}&=\min(v_{\Phi_d}(\alpha_m),v_{\Phi_d}(\beta_m)),\\ e_{N,d}&=\min_{\sigma\in S_N}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}t_{i+\sigma(i),d}. \end{aligned} The last expression is a minimum-cost assignment: row ii is matched to column σ(i)\sigma(i) at cost ti+σ(i),dt_{i+\sigma(i),d}. The valuation of a polynomial in YY means the minimum valuation of its coefficients in ℚ[p]\mathbb{Q}[p]. Each determinant term is divisible by ΦdeN,d\Phi_d^{e_{N,d}}. An exact calculation outside Lean gives the following monic contents. For the table, an exact program computes the full polynomials ℋN(Y0;p)\mathcal H_N(Y_0;p) at Y0=0,…,NY_0=0,\ldots,N by fraction-free elimination, checking every polynomial division. Their monic gcd in ℚ[p]\mathbb{Q}[p] is cont⁡YℋN\operatorname{cont}_Y\mathcal H_N: evaluation gives one divisibility direction, and interpolation of the degree-at-most-NN polynomial in YY gives the other. The calculation includes every factor, not just a prescribed list of cyclotomic candidates.

The same program produces a nonzero residue witness for every pair 1≤N≤8,1≤d≤max⁡(8,2N−2).1\le N\le8,\qquad 1\le d\le\max(8,2N-2). There are 7676 such pairs. For each, the certificate gives an optimal assignment, integer dual potentials, an integer Y0∈{0,…,N}Y_0\in\{0,\ldots,N\} and the nonzero residue ΓN,d(Y0)\Gamma_{N,d}(Y_0). The signed minimum-cost subset recurrence and the determinant of the reduced matrix give the same residue. A separate check computes the full polynomial ℋN(Y0;p)\mathcal H_N(Y_0;p) and verifies directly that division by ΦdeN,d\Phi_d^{e_{N,d}} leaves exactly this nonzero residue. At N=2,d=1N=2,d=1, for example, the entry valuations are (0225)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&2\\2&5\end{smallmatrix}\right), e2,1=4e_{2,1}=4, and Γ2,1(0)=−9\Gamma_{2,1}(0)=-9.

The source coefficients, determinant-value polynomials and witnesses are computed by that program, which also repeats the direct determinant checks; its recorded result lists every witness. At ranks six to eight these certificates cover only the stated cyclotomic-index window; complete coefficient contents are computed only through rank five.

These computations distinguish systematic common factors from cancellation beyond entry valuations, a distinction also important in fraction-free matrix decompositions [38]. In particular the gcd argument at the points 0,…,N0,\ldots,N is over ℚ[p]\mathbb{Q}[p]: the rational Vandermonde inverse is not generally integral, so it must not be used to assert the corresponding coefficient gcd in ℤ[p]\mathbb{Z}[p].

Proposition 4 of Krattenthaler–Rochev–Väänänen–Zudilin obtains cyclotomic factors through root-of-unity annihilation for a different first-order tail recurrence. No corresponding recurrence has been established for this moving-diagonal pencil. The finite witnesses prove equality with the assignment bound at these 7676 pairs. They do not exclude excess at larger ranks or, at ranks six to eight, cyclotomic indices outside the stated window. Whether minimum-valuation residues ever cancel systematically, and whether sms_m is a Stieltjes sequence, remain separate questions. The remainder measure answers neither.

Rescaling integer rows

Fix a rational base a/b>1a/b>1. An irrationality argument constructs integer-coefficient forms in 11 and F(a/b)F(a/b) that are nonzero and tend to zero. Bounds on coefficient height help construct those forms or bound an irrationality exponent, but height times error need not tend to zero for the one-form irrationality criterion. An integer row (U,V)(U,V) is primitive when gcd⁡(|U|,|V|)=1\gcd(|U|,|V|)=1. Dividing a nonzero row by this gcd divides its remainder by the same integer. For an integer coefficient pair (U,V)(U,V) and a real target SS, put LS(U,V)=US−V,Δ((Un,Vn),(Um,Vm))=UnVm−UmVn.L_S(U,V)=US-V, \qquad \Delta\bigl((U_n,V_n),(U_m,V_m)\bigr)=U_nV_m-U_mV_n. We call LS(U,V)L_S(U,V) the error of the row at SS; a good approximation is one that makes it small. The second expression is their 2×22\times2 determinant. It eliminates SS exactly: Δ=UmLS(Un,Vn)−UnLS(Um,Vm).\Delta=U_mL_S(U_n,V_n)-U_nL_S(U_m,V_m).

If this integer determinant does not vanish, then 1≤|Δ|≤|Um||LS(Un,Vn)|+|Un||LS(Um,Vm)|,1\le|\Delta| \le|U_m|\,\bigl|L_S(U_n,V_n)\bigr|+|U_n|\,\bigl|L_S(U_m,V_m)\bigr|, and the two errors cannot both be smaller than 1/(|Un|+|Um|)1/(|U_n|+|U_m|). The next theorem compares the divisor introduced by rescaling with the resulting change in the determinant’s absolute value.

Theorem 4.1 (rescaling rows and their determinant). Let SS be real, let (Un,Vn)(U_n,V_n) and (Um,Vm)(U_m,V_m) be pairs of integers, and let cn,cmc_n,c_m be integers. Then LS(cnUn,cnVn)=cnLS(Un,Vn),L_S(c_nU_n,c_nV_n)=c_nL_S(U_n,V_n), Δ(cn(Un,Vn),cm(Um,Vm))=cncmΔ((Un,Vn),(Um,Vm)),\Delta\bigl(c_n(U_n,V_n),c_m(U_m,V_m)\bigr) =c_nc_m\Delta\bigl((U_n,V_n),(U_m,V_m)\bigr), and consequently |Δ(cn(Un,Vn),cm(Um,Vm))|=|cn||cm||Δ((Un,Vn),(Um,Vm))|.\left|\Delta\bigl(c_n(U_n,V_n),c_m(U_m,V_m)\bigr)\right| =|c_n|\,|c_m|\, \left|\Delta\bigl((U_n,V_n),(U_m,V_m)\bigr)\right|. In particular cncmc_nc_m divides the scaled determinant. Multiplication by these scalars therefore introduces a divisor whose absolute value is exactly the factor multiplying the determinant’s absolute value.

Proof. Expand the linear form and use the bilinearity of the determinant. The original integer determinant is the quotient witnessing divisibility; it need not be primitive. ◻

Example 4.2. Take (Un,Vn)=(1,2)(U_n,V_n)=(1,2) and (Um,Vm)=(3,5)(U_m,V_m)=(3,5), so that Δ=1⋅5−3⋅2=−1\Delta=1\cdot5-3\cdot2=-1. Multiplying the first row by cn=6c_n=6 and the second by cm=10c_m=10 gives the rows (6,12)(6,12) and (30,50)(30,50), whose determinant is 6⋅50−30⋅12=−606\cdot50-30\cdot12=-60. That determinant is now divisible by 6060, which looks like a local gain of 6060; and its absolute value has risen from 11 to 6060, which is a cost of exactly the same size.

Lean checks the error identity in error scaling, the determinant identity in content factorisation, the exact absolute-height identity in absolute determinant scaling, the divisor statement in content-product divisibility, and the elimination identity in exterior determinant identity.

The identities allow zero scalars, but cancelling the scalar factors requires them to be nonzero. Multiplication alone gives no improvement in the comparison between a divisor and the determinant’s absolute value. The theorem neither asserts that the determinant is nonzero nor estimates the original approximation error. Cancelling polynomial factors before evaluation, finding factors common to several minors, and adding different rows remain separate operations.

Congruences after evaluation at 3/23/2

The polynomials in Zudilin’s construction give integer rows after evaluation and denominator clearing [8]. The next results apply to arbitrary polynomials in ℤ[X]\mathbb{Z}[X], not just those polynomials. We first compute the evaluated integers modulo 22 and 33, then count their possible residues modulo powers of these primes. The tools are elementary congruences, the pigeonhole principle and Bézout’s identity. The final scalar inequality, Theorem 5.12, concerns the parameters of Zudilin’s construction rather than its coefficient polynomials.

Substituting X=3/2X=3/2 into an integer polynomial produces a rational number whose denominator is cleared by a sufficiently large power of 22. To use the same operation when adding polynomials, first fix a truncation index W≥0W\ge0. For P(X)=∑ipiXi∈ℤ[X]P(X)=\sum_i p_iX^i\in\mathbb{Z}[X], put HW(P)=∑i=0Wpi3i2W−i.H_W(P)=\sum_{i=0}^{W}p_i\,3^i2^{W-i}. This is the denominator-cleared evaluation at 3/23/2. Each term piXip_iX^i with i≤Wi\le W contributes pi3i2W−ip_i3^i2^{W-i}. Keep the index WW fixed when polynomials are added. When W≥deg⁡PW\ge\deg P, this is exactly the cleared numerator, since ∑i=0Wpi3i2W−i=2W∑i=0Wpi(32)i=2WP(32).\sum_{i=0}^{W}p_i\,3^i2^{W-i}=2^{W}\sum_{i=0}^{W}p_i\left(\tfrac32\right)^{i} =2^{W}P\!\left(\tfrac32\right).

Here a unit coefficient in ℤ\mathbb{Z} means 11 or −1-1. Thus a monic polynomial of degree WW with constant term ±1\pm1 satisfies both unit conditions below. Those conditions are sufficient, not necessary: the congruences themselves only require that the relevant coefficient not be divisible by the relevant prime.

Theorem 5.1 (endpoint residues). Let P=∑ipiXi∈ℤ[X]P=\sum_ip_iX^i\in\mathbb{Z}[X] and let W≥0W\ge0. Then HW(P)≡p02W(mod⁡3),HW(P)≡pW3W(mod⁡2).H_W(P)\equiv p_0\,2^W\pmod 3,\qquad H_W(P)\equiv p_W\,3^W\pmod 2. Consequently a unit constant coefficient prevents divisibility by 33, and a unit coefficient at index WW prevents divisibility by 22.

Proof. Modulo 33, every summand with i>0i>0 vanishes; modulo 22, every summand with i<Wi<W vanishes. The remaining powers are units in the corresponding residue fields. ◻

Since 2W2^{W} is invertible modulo 33 and 3W3^{W} is invertible modulo 22, the two congruences say more than the stated consequence: divisibility of HW(P)H_W(P) by 33 is decided by p0p_0 alone, and divisibility by 22 by pWp_W alone. The rest of the coefficient vector is invisible to both primes. The coefficient pWp_W is the top coefficient of PP exactly when deg⁡P=W\deg P=W, and is zero when deg⁡P<W\deg P<W. The identity HW(P)=2WP(3/2)H_W(P)=2^{W}P(3/2) is guaranteed when deg⁡P≤W\deg P\le W. Without a degree bound, increasing the truncation index gives HW+1(P)=2HW(P)+pW+13W+1,H_{W+1}(P)=2H_W(P)+p_{W+1}3^{W+1}, so the truncated sum doubles precisely when the extra coefficient is zero.
